analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card interest rates at 18% for everyone.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a Senate committee hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act to bar credit card companies from charging an annual interest rate above 18%, including all finance charges. It also blocks issuers from loading on extra fees to get around the cap, and lets borrowers sue card companies that break the rule. It sat in the Senate Banking Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of Americans who carry a credit card balance. Average credit card rates have run well above 20%, so a hard 18% ceiling — with fees counted toward it — would directly cut borrowing costs for anyone carrying debt from month to month. People with lower credit scores, who are charged the highest rates, would see the biggest savings.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on credit card credit at 18%, including all finance charges.
Prevents creditors from imposing fees not counted as finance charges in order to evade the cap, and limits the total of such fees to the total finance charges assessed.
Exposes creditors that violate the cap to civil liability under section 130 of the Truth in Lending Act, giving borrowers a way to recover damages.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — largely large banks and finance companies — would lose interest and fee revenue on the roughly half of card accounts that revolve a balance. Some of that cost could be passed back to consumers in other forms: tighter approval standards, lower credit limits, or reduced rewards programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit card issuers and big banks

drawbacks.text: A rate cap is a ceiling, not a subsidy: issuers who can no longer price for risk may respond by denying cards or limiting credit to borrowers with poor credit, who currently pay the highest rates. Some higher-risk borrowers could lose access to credit entirely rather than see cheaper credit.

Card issuers often fund rewards programs, grace periods, and no-annual-fee cards out of interest and interchange revenue; a binding cap could shrink those perks for everyone, including borrowers who pay in full each month.

The bill received no committee action and no Congressional Budget Office cost estimate, so there was never a formal analysis of how much interest revenue would shift or how credit access would change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households that carry credit card debt month to month, the benefit is direct and large: a legal ceiling on a rate that routinely runs above 20%, with anti-evasion language so fees cannot be repackaged as interest, and a private right of action to enforce it. The main honest cost falls on borrowers with the weakest credit, for whom a price cap can mean no credit at all, and indirectly on all cardholders through rewards and fees. On balance the bill favors indebted households over card issuers, though it was never debated, so these tradeoffs were never tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Josh Hawley introduced the bill on September 11, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers kept charging rates above 18% with no cap, and no member of the Senate besides Hawley put their name on the effort. Indebted households gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers and their shareholders

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Missouri; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 11, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing or markup was ever scheduled in the 16 months before the Congress ended.

against.name: Card issuers and the banking industry
against.role: Credit card banks and finance companies whose interest and fee revenue the 18% cap would cut
against.what_they_did: Opposed rate-cap legislation as a matter of industry position; rate caps of this kind drew opposition from the banking lobby in the 118th Congress, and no committee action followed.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so there is no roll-call record; its single sponsor was a Republican in a chamber whose Banking Committee majority was Democratic, and no member of either party joined him.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (large banks and finance companies)
industries.note: An 18% hard cap, inclusive of finance charges and with anti-evasion fee limits, would directly cut the interest and fee revenue issuers earn on revolving balances, which run above 20% for a large share of cardholders. The industry's gain from the bill's death was the public's cost in higher borrowing costs.
